body:
<!-- plain-summary -->
Wyrd has a garbage collector that reclaims the disk space left behind by deleted files. It is written, tested, and correct — and the running custodian **never calls it**. So in a real deployment, the space behind every deleted file is never reclaimed. Disks fill with data nobody can reach.

## What

`crates/server/src/custodian.rs` drives the deployable custodian, and **both** of its reconcile passes hand `None` where the GC context goes:

```rust
.reconcile_pass(zone, custodian, None /* gc */, Some(&scrub_ctx), None, None, clock())
.reconcile_pass(zone, custodian, None /* gc */, None, Some(&ctx), None, clock())
```

`grep -rn "GcContext {" crates/server/src/` returns **nothing** — the deployed role never constructs one. GC runs only under `cargo test`.

This is *acknowledged* in `crates/custodian/src/gc.rs` ("this is **not** a deployed custodian process … standing up the host that drives the loop against live stores is a later slice"), but as far as I can find it is not tracked by an open issue — so it reads as deferred, not as a live production defect. It is a live production defect.

## Why it matters

GC is the **only** thing that reclaims fragment bytes. The delete path explicitly defers the byte reclaim to it (`write.rs:330-331`, referenced from `gc.rs`). So today, on a real cluster:

- **Every delete leaks.** The chunk map goes, the fragments stay, forever.
- **Every completed reconstruction leaks** the fragment it displaced.
- **Every rebalance leaks** the fragment it moved off the draining server.
- Storage grows monotonically with churn, and nothing reclaims it. There is no cleanup path an operator can run either — see #551.

For a storage system, "deleting a file frees no space, ever" is a defect of the first order, and it is invisible until the disks fill.

## Scope

- [ ] Construct a `GcContext` in the deployed custodian (the fleet is already assembled by `connect_fleet`, and the metadata store is already open — the pieces are all there) and pass `Some(&gc)` into a reconcile pass.
- [ ] Decide the **grace window** honestly. `GcContext::grace_window_millis` is documented as *derived from reader version-hold / lease semantics by the caller*, not a magic constant. That derivation is the real work of this issue: too short and GC can tear an in-flight reader; too long and the leak merely slows.
- [ ] Order it against scrub/reconstruction in the pass sequence (GC must not race the repair loop's placement rewrites).
- [ ] A test that drives the **deployed role** (not the library loop) over a store with a deleted file and asserts the bytes are actually reclaimed — the gap here is precisely that the library loop is well-tested and the *wiring* is not.

## Relationship to #551

#551 (post-restore reconciliation) supplies the *evidence* GC needs to reclaim post-restore strays. **That fix cannot take effect until this one lands** — marking a fragment collectable is inert if nothing ever collects. The two are complementary: this issue makes GC run; #551 makes it able to see the fragments a restore stranded.

## Refs

Found while implementing #551. `crates/custodian/src/gc.rs` (the loop, and its "not deployed" note), `crates/server/src/custodian.rs:406,420` (the `None`s), ADR-0005 §288-295.

title: The GC loop is never run by the deployed custodian — reclaimable fragments leak on every delete
